claim: Planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling controls the polarization of cells within the plane of an epithelium.
source: Planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling controls the polarization of cells within the plane of an epithelium.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about PCP signaling that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Two molecular modules composed of Fat(Ft)/Dachsous(Ds)/Four-jointed(Fj) and a 'PCP-core' including Frizzled(Fz) and Dishevelled(Dsh) contribute to polarization of individual cells.
source: Two molecular modules composed of Fat(Ft)/Dachsous(Ds)/Four-jointed(Fj) and a 'PCP-core' including Frizzled(Fz) and Dishevelled(Dsh) contribute to polarization of individual cells.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the molecular components of PCP signaling.

claim: The Ft/Ds/Fj-module has an effect on a MT-cytoskeleton.
source: Consistent with previous results, we find that the Ft/Ds/Fj-module has an effect on a MT-cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous results and is consistent with data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Ft/Ds/Fj-module provides directional information to the core-module through MT organizing function.
source: Here, we provide evidence for the model that the Ft/Ds/Fj-module provides directional information to the core-module through this MT organizing function.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the paper, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The apical MT-cytoskeleton shows Ft/Ds/Fj-dependent initial polarization prior to global alignment of the core-module.
source: We show Ft/Ds/Fj-dependent initial polarization of the apical MT-cytoskeleton prior to global alignment of the core-module
evidence: This temporal relationship is demonstrated through imaging data at different developmental stages shown in the figures.

claim: The anchoring of apical non-centrosomal MTs at apical junctions is polarized.
source: reveal that the anchoring of apical non-centrosomal MTs at apical junctions is polarized
evidence: This is supported by TEM data and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Directional trafficking of vesicles containing Dsh depends on Ft.
source: observe that directional trafficking of vesicles containing Dsh depends on Ft
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging experiments comparing wildtype and ft mutant tissue shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the fly wing epithelium, Frizzled, Dishevelled and Diego become enriched at the distal adherens junctions.
source: In the fly wing epithelium, three of the six proteins, Frizzled, Dishevelled and Diego (Dgo), become enriched at the distal adherens junctions (AJ)
evidence: This is established knowledge about core PCP protein localization, supported by citation (Axelrod, 2009).

claim: Van Gogh and Prickle localize to the proximal side of cells in the fly wing epithelium.
source: two, Van Gogh (Vang) and Prickle (Pk) localize to the proximal side
evidence: This is established knowledge about core PCP protein localization, supported by citation (Axelrod, 2009).

claim: Starry night/Flamingo localizes to both proximal and distal sides of cells in the fly wing epithelium.
source: while Starry night/Flamingo (Fmi) localizes to both proximal and distal sides (Axelrod, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge about core PCP protein localization, supported by citation.

claim: Preferential interactions between Fmi/Fz and Fmi/Vang complexes across cell boundaries can account for intracellular segregation of these complexes.
source: Preferential interactions between Fmi/Fz and Fmi/Vang complexes across cell boundaries (Lawrence et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2008; Strutt and Strutt, 2008) and intercellular feedback loops (Tree et al., 2002; Amonlirdviman et al., 2005) can account for intracellular segregation of these complexes and coordinated alignment among neighboring cells.
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Intercellular feedback loops can account for coordinated alignment among neighboring cells.
source: Preferential interactions between Fmi/Fz and Fmi/Vang complexes across cell boundaries (Lawrence et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2008; Strutt and Strutt, 2008) and intercellular feedback loops (Tree et al., 2002; Amonlirdviman et al., 2005) can account for intracellular segregation of these complexes and coordinated alignment among neighboring cells.
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The Ft/Ds/Fj system acts as a 'global' PCP module, transducing tissue level directional cues encoded by opposing Ds and Fj expression gradients.
source: It is proposed that the Ft/Ds/Fj system, comprising the atypical cadherins Ft (Yang et al., 2002), Ds (Adler et al., 1998) and the Golgi-resident protein Fj (Zeidler et al., 1999), acts as a 'global' PCP module, transducing tissue level directional cues encoded by opposing Ds and Fj expression gradients, to orient the core PCP module (Yang et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the Drosophila pupal wing, apical non-centrosomal MTs are aligned along the proximal distal axis prior to the onset of hair growth.
source: In the Drosophila pupal wing, apical non-centrosomal MTs are aligned along the proximal distal axis prior to the onset of hair growth (Fristrom and Fristrom, 1975; Eaton et al., 1996; Turner and Adler, 1998; Shimada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Ft/Ds/Fj module plays a role in organization of apical MTs.
source: The Ft/Ds/Fj module plays an incompletely defined role in organization of these MTs (Harumoto et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MT-associated vesicles containing Fz preferentially move in a plus-end directed fashion toward the distal cell cortex.
source: MT-associated vesicles containing Fz are observed to preferentially move in a plus-end directed fashion toward the distal cell cortex (Shimada et al., 2006)
evidence: This observation is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Core PCP protein polarization with respect to the tissue axes is first observed during larval wing development.
source: Core PCP protein polarization with respect to the tissue axes is first observed during larval wing development (Classen et al., 2005).
evidence: This temporal observation is supported by citation.

claim: The earliest evident apical tubulin staining was seen in early to mid third-instar.
source: The earliest evident apical tubulin staining was seen in early to mid third-instar, and revealed an asymmetrical accumulation of tubulin in mostly single 'dots' within each cell (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the authors' experiments, supported by imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: Tubulin dots show a significant bias of localizing on the proximal side of the cell.
source: Image analysis of the tubulin dots revealed a significant bias of dots localizing on the proximal side of the cell (side closest to the hinge fold; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–A″).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative image analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Early MTs appear as dense bundles anchored to proximal junctions in EM images.
source: In EM images, these early MTs appear as dense bundles anchored to proximal junctions (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from TEM data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MTs are strongly aligned along the evolving P/D axis throughout wing development.
source: Throughout wing development, image analysis software ('Materials and methods') applied to fluorescence images demonstrated that MTs are strongly aligned along the evolving P/D axis
evidence: This is supported by quantitative image analysis of fluorescence data throughout development.

claim: The orientation of MTs is reflected in the evolving pattern of polarized PCP proteins.
source: the orientation of MTs was reflected in the evolving pattern of polarized PCP proteins, from the radial pattern (P/D polarity vectors from hinge fold toward center of wing pouch, resulting in concentric circles of P/D cell boundaries) evident in third instar and early pupal stage (Figure 1C′–D′) to the parallel pattern of 19–30 hAPF pupal wings that presages the hair polarity pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B″–D″; Strutt et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2003; Matakatsu and Blair, 2004; Classen et al., 2005; Rogulja et al., 2008; Aigouy et al., 2010; Hogan et al., 2011; Sagner et al., 2012).
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated through imaging data and supported by multiple citations.

claim: At the time the MT dots appear, there is no evident core PCP protein asymmetry.
source: Importantly, at the time the MT dots appear, there is no evident core PCP protein asymmetry
evidence: This temporal observation is based on imaging data comparing MT and core protein localization.

claim: Core PCP asymmetry becomes globally aligned along the P/D axis only after apical junction-anchored MTs appear.
source: whereas core PCP asymmetry becomes globally aligned along the P/D axis in slightly older discs only after apical junction-anchored MTs appear (Figure 1A–C), consistent with a requirement of the apical MT cytoskeleton for core module alignment.
evidence: This temporal sequence is demonstrated through imaging data at different developmental stages.

claim: TEM of 24 hr wings confirmed the previously described polarized organization of MTs that reach across the cell.
source: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) of 24 hr wings confirmed the previously described polarized organization of MTs that reach across the cell (Eaton et al., 1996; Shimada et al., 2006; Harumoto et al., 2010; Figure 2A)
evidence: This is confirmed by TEM data shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Associations of planar MTs with apical intercellular junctions form juxtaposed, intercellular structures with MT anchoring sites on adjacent membranes of neighboring cells.
source: and also revealed that the previously observed associations of planar MTs with apical intercellular junctions (Fristrom and Fristrom, 1975) form juxtaposed, intercellular structures with MT anchoring sites on adjacent membranes of neighboring cells (Figure 2A,C–E).
evidence: This structural observation is demonstrated by TEM data shown in Figure 2.

claim: MT anchoring sites were preferentially observed at P/D cell boundaries.
source: These anchoring sites were preferentially observed at P/D cell boundaries (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of TEM data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EM images showed no association of centrosomes with MTs in non-dividing cells throughout wing development.
source: EM images showed no association of centrosomes with MTs in non-dividing cells throughout wing development, suggesting that apical MTs are nucleated elsewhere (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from TEM data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Apical MTs are nucleated elsewhere than centrosomes.
source: EM images showed no association of centrosomes with MTs in non-dividing cells throughout wing development, suggesting that apical MTs are nucleated elsewhere (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of centrosome-MT associations in TEM data.

claim: Patronin is detected inside the cell, but not at the cell cortex.
source: We detected the minus-end binding proteins γ-tubulin and Patronin (Stearns and Kirschner, 1994; Goodwin and Vale, 2010) inside the cell, but not at the cell cortex, where they have been observed in other contexts (Meng et al., 2008; Feldman and Priess, 2012; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Patronin knockdown shows no PCP phenotype.
source: Consistent with this, patronin knockdown (Mummery-Widmer et al., 2009) shows no PCP phenotype.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation.

claim: β-catenin (Armadillo), α-catenin and PAR-1 are present symmetrically at the cell cortex.
source: MT associated proteins β-catenin (Armadillo) (Ligon et al., 2001; McCartney et al., 2001), α-catenin (McCartney et al., 2001) and PAR-1 (Doerflinger et al., 2003; Harumoto et al., 2010) are all present symmetrically at the cell cortex but did not show asymmetric localization at the AJs
evidence: This is based on immunostaining observations and supported by citations.

claim: MTs are generally aligned with Ds and Fj gradients from their first appearance in third instar discs.
source: Here, our analysis shows that MTs are generally aligned with Ds and Fj gradients from their first appearance in third instar discs (Rogulja et al., 2008), when they emerge on proximal sides of the cell cortex (Figure 1A).
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated through imaging data and supported by citation.

claim: Throughout larval wing discs and pupal wings, MT orientation correlates with the direction of Ds and Fj gradients.
source: Throughout larval wing discs and pupal wings, MT orientation correlates with the direction of Ds and Fj gradients (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated through imaging data across developmental stages.

claim: In imaginal discs, marked subcellular asymmetry of Ft localization is observed that substantially overlaps core protein distribution.
source: As noted previously (Brittle et al., 2012), in imaginal discs, when the tissue is small and gradients appear to be steeper (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), marked subcellular asymmetry of Ft localization is observed that substantially overlaps core protein distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data and citation.

claim: The steepest regions of the Ds and Fj gradients correspond to the most polarized MTs.
source: The steepest regions of the gradients correspond to the most polarized MTs (compare Figure 1D to Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated by comparing imaging data from different figures.

claim: Ds and Fj gradients are appropriately aligned to polarize the MT cytoskeleton and thereby bias core PCP protein polarization from its earliest appearance.
source: Therefore, Ds and Fj gradients are appropriately aligned to polarize the MT cytoskeleton and thereby bias core PCP protein polarization from its earliest appearance.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatiotemporal correlation data presented.

claim: At 24 hAPF, MTs in the proximal and central part of the wing in FtΔECDΔN-1 rescued flies were randomized.
source: At 24 hAPF, MTs in the proximal and central part of the wing, where hair polarity is often disturbed, were randomized (Figure 3A,A′, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A,A′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantitative analysis shown in the figures.

claim: In peripheral regions of FtΔECDΔN-1 rescued wings, MTs were ordered and oriented with the hairs and core PCP domains.
source: In these peripheral regions, MTs were ordered and oriented with the hairs and core PCP domains (Figure 3A″).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 3A″.

claim: Flies in which the Ds and Fj gradients were removed showed an essentially identical phenotype to FtΔECDΔN-1 rescued flies.
source: Flies in which the Ds and Fj gradients were removed showed an essentially identical phenotype (ds38k fjN7/dsUA071 fjd1; UAS-Ds/TubP-Gal4; Figure 3—figure supplement 5B–B″).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data comparing different genotypes.

claim: MT orientation was randomized in ft or ds clones in the proximal part of the wing.
source: Finally, MT orientation was randomized in ft or ds clones in the same proximal part of the wing where it is disturbed in ft mutant wings rescued for Hippo signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C; see also [Ma et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data and supported by citation.

claim: In the central part of pupal wings, MT orientation, core PCP protein polarity and adult polarity are strongly dependent on PCP signaling through Ft.
source: These data show that in the central part of pupal wings, MT orientation, core PCP protein polarity and adult polarity are strongly dependent on PCP signaling through Ft (Figure 3—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: An additional signal, perhaps from the wing margin, can orient MTs in the periphery of the wing.
source: They also suggest the existence of an additional signal, perhaps from the wing margin, that can orient MTs in the periphery of the wing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that peripheral MTs remain oriented in Ft/Ds/Fj mutants.

claim: In cells surrounding ft clones in wing discs, nascent MT bundles are inappropriately polarized toward the cell border abutting the mutant cells.
source: In cells surrounding ft clones in wing discs, where unopposed Ds within the clone is expected to recruit excess Ft to the neighboring cell boundaries, nascent MT bundles are inappropriately polarized toward the cell border abutting the mutant cells (Figure 3B,B′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 3B,B′.

claim: In pupal wings, MTs are perpendicular to ft clone boundaries.
source: Similarly, in pupal wings MTs are perpendicular to the clone boundary (Figure 3C,C″)
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C,C″.

claim: Ft and Ds are both required and instructive for MT organization.
source: Therefore, Ft and Ds are both required and instructive for MT organization.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the clone experiments showing reorganization of MTs around mutant tissue.

claim: Distally biased microtubule-dependent trafficking of Fz-containing vesicles occurs during polarization of the core PCP proteins.
source: Distally biased microtubule (MT)-dependent trafficking of Fz-containing vesicles has been shown to occur during polarization of the core PCP proteins, and both are sensitive to MT disruption, suggesting that transport is required for polarization (Shimada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The majority of Dsh::GFP vesicles (80%) moved along the P/D axis.
source: The majority of vesicles (80%, n = 1192) moved along the P/D axis, and showed a significant though modest bias towards distal vs proximal transport (Figure 4A,C–D; Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: Dsh::GFP vesicles showed a significant though modest bias towards distal vs proximal transport.
source: The majority of vesicles (80%, n = 1192) moved along the P/D axis, and showed a significant though modest bias towards distal vs proximal transport (Figure 4A,C–D; Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Dsh::GFP vesicles commonly emerged from one side of the cell and were transported directly across the length of the cell to be incorporated into the membrane of an opposing cellular face.
source: First, and most commonly, vesicles emerged from one side of the cell and were transported directly across the length of the cell to be incorporated into the membrane of an opposing cellular face (Figure 4A′; Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging data.

claim: A minority of Dsh::GFP vesicles took staggered paths without directional bias, paused frequently, and often left the apical plane of the cell.
source: Second, a minority of Dsh::GFP vesicles took staggered paths without directional bias, paused frequently, and often left the apical plane of the cell (Figure 4B,B′; Video 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging data.

claim: Only a minor fraction of Dsh vesicles co-stains with the early endosome marker Rab5 or exocyst protein Sec5.
source: Consistently, in fixed specimens, only a minor fraction of Dsh vesicles co-stains with the early endosome marker Rab5 or exocyst protein Sec5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunostaining data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: A minority of Dsh vesicles moves through the recycling pathway while the majority appears to be part of a transcytosis pathway.
source: Thus, a minority of vesicles moves through the recycling pathway while the majority of Dsh vesicles appears to be part of a transcytosis pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the different movement patterns and marker colocalization data.

claim: There is no directionally biased trafficking of Vang::YFP vesicles.
source: In contrast, we see no directionally biased trafficking of Vang::YFP vesicles (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The 'distal' components Fz and Dsh, but not 'proximal' components, are subject to directional trafficking.
source: Together with prior data, our observations suggest that the 'distal' components Fz and Dsh, but not 'proximal' components, are subject to directional trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the current data on Dsh and Vang trafficking combined with prior data on Fz.

claim: In ft mutant pupal wing tissue, Dsh::GFP vesicles moved much shorter distances (or showed no net movement), without directional bias, and lacked processivity.
source: We observed that, in comparison to wildtype cells, vesicles moved much shorter distances (or showed no net movement), without directional bias, and lacked processivity, instead taking random paths with frequent direction changes (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of live imaging data in ft mutant tissue shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Apical MTs are oriented independent of core PCP mutants fz, vang and dsh1.
source: Apical MTs are oriented independent of core PCP mutants fz (Shimada et al., 2006; Harumoto et al., 2010), vang (Harumoto et al., 2010) and dsh1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data and supported by citations.

claim: Most Dsh1::GFP vesicles move along the P-D axis in dsh1 flies.
source: We found that, unlike in ft mutant cells, most Dsh1::GFP vesicles move along the P-D axis (Figure 4G; Video 4)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Oriented trafficking does not depend on core protein asymmetry.
source: consistent with the presence of oriented MTs, and indicating that oriented trafficking does not depend on core protein asymmetry.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Dsh1 vesicles show oriented movement in dsh1 mutants lacking core protein asymmetry.

claim: Apical planar MTs that direct biased transcytosis of Dsh depend on the Ft/Ds/Fj pathway, but not on core module function.
source: These results show that apical planar MTs that direct biased transcytosis of Dsh depend on the Ft/Ds/Fj pathway, but not on core module function.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experiments showing oriented MTs and trafficking in core mutants but not in Ft/Ds/Fj mutants.

claim: Dsh and Fz vesicles may be at least partially distinct populations.
source: Furthermore, the movement of Dsh1 vesicles, the faster kinetics of transcytosing Dsh vesicles, and the greater processivity, compared to Fz vesicles all suggest that Dsh and Fz vesicles may be at least partially distinct populations.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the properties of Dsh and Fz vesicle trafficking.

claim: Oppositely oriented linear gradients of Ds and Fj polarize a field of cells with similar kinetics and identical steady state levels of polarization across the entire field in simulation.
source: In simulation, oppositely oriented linear gradients of Ds and Fj polarize a field of cells with similar kinetics and identical steady state levels of polarization across the entire field.
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling simulations.

claim: Simulation of a linear gradient, a step gradient, or a steep proximal Ds gradient and a shallow or flat distal gradient produces identical levels of steady state polarization across the field and similar proximal and distal kinetics.
source: Notably, simulation of a linear gradient, a step gradient, or a steep proximal Ds gradient and a shallow or flat distal gradient produces identical levels of steady state polarization across the field and similar proximal and distal kinetics, showing that the mechanism is not expected to be very sensitive to the precise shape of the Ds gradient (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Propagation of Ft-Ds polarity into an adjacent shallow or flat region is weak, and limited to two columns of cells.
source: In the cases of a steep local Ds gradient, propagation of Ft-Ds polarity into an adjacent shallow or flat region is weak, and limited to two columns of cells (data not shown), most likely due to absence of a robust feedback mechanism in our model.
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling simulations.

claim: Propagation of Ft-Ds polarization in vivo is much weaker than that of the core PCP mechanism.
source: Similarly, propagation of Ft-Ds polarization in vivo is seen to be much weaker than that of the core PCP mechanism (c.f. Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Distal polarity is independent of Ft function.
source: Distal (peripheral) polarity is independent of Ft function; polarity in this region may depend on a spatial signal perhaps originating from the wing margin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that peripheral regions maintain polarity in Ft mutants.

claim: Wnt4 overexpression reorganizes MTs.
source: Notably Wnt4 (but not Wg) overexpression reorganizes MTs (Figure 3—figure supplement 7)
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: A polarized MT cytoskeleton orients PCP throughout wing development by directing the trafficking of Dsh containing vesicles.
source: Together, our findings support the hypothesis that a polarized MT cytoskeleton orients PCP throughout wing development by directing the trafficking of Dsh containing vesicles.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Ft/Ds/Fj PCP module directs orientation of the apical MT cytoskeleton, at least in the proximal central portion of the wing.
source: Furthermore, they confirm that the Ft/Ds/Fj PCP module directs orientation of this apical MT cytoskeleton, at least in the proximal central portion of the wing.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental evidence showing MT disorganization in Ft/Ds/Fj mutants.

claim: A second signal, acting near the wing margin and perhaps originating from the margin, can also organize MTs to orient the core PCP mechanism.
source: We infer that a second signal, acting near the wing margin and perhaps originating from the margin, can also organize MTs to orient the core PCP mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that peripheral MTs remain oriented in Ft/Ds/Fj mutants.

claim: In third instar wings, when the tissue is smaller, the two signals (Ft/Ds/Fj and margin signal) are largely redundant.
source: We propose that in third instar wings, when the tissue is smaller, the two signals are largely redundant, so that defects in Hippo-rescued ft mutants are limited to the most proximal regions (Feng and Irvine, 2007; Brittle et al., 2012; Matakatsu and Blair, 2012; Pan et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: In larger pupal and adult wings, Hippo-rescued ft mutants show larger regions of disturbed polarity.
source: whereas in larger pupal and adult wings, Hippo-rescued ft mutants show larger regions of disturbed polarity.
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing phenotypes at different developmental stages.

claim: Even in regions well polarized by the presumed wing margin signal, ectopic Ds expression can reorganize polarity.
source: Notably, even in regions well polarized by the presumed wing margin signal, ectopic Ds expression can reorganize polarity (Matakatsu and Blair, 2004; Harumoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The strong correspondence of MT orientation and core protein orientation throughout wing morphogenesis suggests that Ds-Fj gradients provide instructional information for core PCP orientation.
source: Furthermore, the strong correspondence of MT orientation and core protein orientation throughout wing morphogenesis, their overall correspondence to Ds-Fj gradients, and the ability of altered Ft or Ds expression patterns to reconfigure MT orientation, suggest that these gradients provide instructional information for core PCP orientation, at least in the proximal and central region of the wing.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatiotemporal correlation data and manipulation experiments.

claim: The Ft/Ds/Fj signal likely acts in conjunction with other molecular signals and perhaps with mechanical inputs such as cell flow and cell elongation.
source: This signal likely acts in conjunction with other molecular signals, particularly in the peripheral region of the wing, and perhaps with mechanical inputs such as cell flow and cell elongation (Aigouy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential additional inputs, supported by citation.

claim: The tissue and compartment specific expression predominance of the Pk vs Spiny-legs isoforms of Pk determines the direction of Ds and Fj gradient interpretation.
source: Recently, it was shown that the tissue and compartment specific expression predominance of the Pk vs Spiny-legs isoforms of Pk determines the direction of Ds and Fj gradient interpretation (Ayukawa et al., 2014; Olofsson and Axelrod, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by recent citations.

claim: The Ft/Ds/Fj global PCP module, together with a partially redundant peripheral wing signal, orients apical polarized microtubules, directing Dsh-vesicle transcytosis, and thereby imparting directional information to the core PCP module.
source: In summary, we provide evidence favoring the model that the Ft/Ds/Fj global PCP module, together with a partially redundant and as yet unidentified peripheral wing signal, orients apical polarized microtubules, directing Dsh-vesicle transcytosis, and thereby imparting directional information to the core PCP module.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarizing the evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of polarized MTs suggests that a MT dependent global cue may also function in vertebrate PCP.
source: The presence of polarized MTs suggests that a MT dependent global cue may also function in vertebrate PCP (Vladar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential conservation of the mechanism, supported by citation.
